newsitem.title: USA: Tough trade talk masks US comfort with strong dlr.
newsitem.headline: Tough trade talk masks US comfort with strong dlr.

text.p: Recent complaints from Treasury officials about Japan's burgeoning bilateral trade surplus mask U.S. comfort with the dollar's stronger levels, currency market players said on Wednesday.
The robust dollar may be taking its toll on domestic exporters, but it has also helped dampen U.S. inflationary pressures, attract capital inflows and reduce upward pressure on interest rates.

Treasury officials are most likely concerned about a stronger dollar's potential for undermining U.S. competitiveness. But these worries are not acute enough to spark concerted efforts to reverse the dollar's rise just yet, experts said.

"You have to separate the official U.S. comments from their true intent," said John Praveen, senior international economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. "I think the administration fully understands and appreciates the value of the strong dollar."
On Wednesday, the dollar rose to its highest level in over four-and-a-half years against the yen and to a three-year peak against the mark.
After climbing sharply during the first month of the year, the dollar's rise stalled in late-February and March, only to resume its push to fresh multi-year highs this week.
Since the beginning of 1997, the dollar has appreciated by almost 10 percent against the yen and by roughly 12 percent against the mark.

Exporters have fingered the dollar's ample gains as the reason for a recent resurgence in Japan's trade surplus with the United States. And ahead of Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's recent trip to Asia, he repeatedly voiced his displeasure with the worsening bilateral trade picture.

But the tough talk appeared to dissipate once Rubin arrived in Japan. Rubin rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency -- and thus a weaker dollar -- was the best way to avoid further gains in Japan's bilateral surplus.
And on his way back from Asia late Tuesday, Rubin denied that his discussions with Japanese officials had involved talk of trying to cap the dollar's advance.
Market sources said Rubin's remarks suggest the administration is fully cognizant of the strong dollar's positive impact on the U.S. economy, but also aware that U.S. exporters must be appeased.

"They may very well be under pressure from automakers and others in Washington political circles," said Merrill Lynch's Praveen. "To blunt their argument, I think the Treasury is trying to preempt more criticism and soften the blow."
Praveen said the dollar's strength carried "asymetric risks," noting its positive impact in Europe and Japan, but questioning the magnitude of its negative implications for the U.S.

He pointed to proprietary studies which showed that recent increases in an import-weighted dollar were larger than those in its export-weighted counterpart, suggesting the greenback's effect in dampening U.S. inflation was greater than its impact in hurting U.S. competitiveness.
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin is one of many U.S. officials who have lauded the beneficial effects of the robust greenback in recent months.

"We're clearly benefitting on the inflation front from the fact that the dollar has moved up quite a lot and our growing imports are cheaper," she said last week, adding that any inflation forecast had to take into account the likely level of the dollar.
Currency traders and analysts said a strong dollar was no substitute for a hike in interest rates, but noted that its impact could not be ignored.

"The strong dollar is Japan's way out of their predicament and on the other side a strong dollar is helping the U.S. from raising interest rates," said Robert Sabia, a vice president on the foreign exchange desk at ING Barings Capital Markets Inc. "It's helping both countries out."
Japan, which is struggling with a recent hike in its consumption tax at a time of economic weakness, is benefitting, along with many European economies, from dollar-induced export-led growth.

Sabia said there were limits to U.S. tolerance for a strong dollar, but echoed other traders and economists who said the pace of the dollar's rise rather than any specific level has generated the most concern.
Another reason for the administration to shy away from curbing dollar gains is recent volatility in U.S. asset markets, analysts said.
Both stocks and bonds swooned following the Federal Reserve's 25 basis point hike in the federal funds rate on March 25, and sudden damage to the dollar could accelerate any slide.

"I would imagine that the administration is not really in a mood to add any more uncertainty to the markets by commenting that the dollar's level might be too high," said David DeRosa, managing partner at Quadrangle Investments, a Connecticut-based hedge fund.
"I believe they have no problem with fluctuations in the dollar that follow fundamentals and there are fundamental reasons for the dollar to be higher."
